design.recommendation:
Short answer. Yes for the review loops, probably for the Backchain loop, no for restructuring the stages. Where the ceiling bites, one-shotting cannot fix it.

What is measured. On Grok medium, planning_review none (option 5) took 20.5 engine minutes (22.05 on the harness clock) against 71.9 for the same-model stage run on 1.21.0. Improve was 45.8 of those 71.9 minutes in the stage run, and 29.2 of 61.3 on GAS. That already meets the 30-minute rule, at 73% of it. The run (noneLive) finished: 52 of 52 rows done, 0 revises, 4 of 4 product checks pass, 18 of 19 script verifications pass. The defects found after planning were each repaired inside the stage that made them, in about 1 to 3 minutes, roughly 10 minutes in total (derived upper bounds) of 91.8. The caveats are n=1, a different release from the 72.7 baseline, and no matched stage-mode run to completion on 0.54.0.

What the data cannot decide. Four things are unmeasured, not zero: the escape rate without review; the quality of unreviewed documents (the none documents are 28 KB against 62 KB, cause unknown, and no blind judge has run); Luna under none; and whether Backchain's one pass earned its 8.4 minutes. Run-to-run variance is about 2x with n=1 per arm.

Luna. none leaves about 172 minutes, and the ledger's floor with no review and no loop is 115 to 131 (estimated). Only volume levers reach 30 there: reasoning share, document size, and effort below xhigh, which has never been run. One-shot options do not.

Ranking.
1. Keep option 5 as the opt-in one-shot lever. Do not flip the default until PT-2 has n=2.
2. Treat option 2 (--backchain-passes none) as the only further candidate. It needs no code and no new carve-out. It is worth 3.7 to 7.3 minutes on Grok (upper bound unverified) and 22 to 57 on Luna (inferred). In noneLive the loop's three findings restated facts already in spec.md, test-strategy.md and environment.md, and nothing after plan read the graph. Do not adopt it on one probe, because the saving is below the run-to-run variance. Measure it in plan-stage output tokens as well as minutes. If the owner wants the loop kept for ownership and trace, option 2b recovers about 3.3 minutes with no gate removed.
3. Option 7 (one combined review after the first RED) is the principled form of 'fix later'. It is unbuilt, so build nothing until PT-3 or a planning-class escape shows a quality loss.

Reject:
- Option 1 (merge stages): at most 0.7 minutes on Grok and about 5 on Luna, with engine churn across 17 suites and a carve-out that has no anchor.
- Option 3 (skip or derive step-plan and test-spec): it deletes the fields the gates run on, conflicts with the owner's primary rule, and moves minutes across the window boundary rather than removing them.
- Option 4 (rolling wave): about 0.3 to 0.6 minutes, and carry-forward already does the learning.
- Option 6 as a package: it stacks carve-outs on the highest-risk combination and still leaves Luna 4 to 5 times over.

Single cheapest next measurement. One more plain `--planning-review none` Grok medium probe on the same build and case, planning only through the W1 test-red accept. It is about 25 minutes of wall time and about $3 by turn-share pro rata ($12.50 over 467 turns; true spend unknown; PT-2's worst-case bound is $45). It completes PT-2's rule (a) and (b) at n=2 and gives the first same-arm variance, which every other comparison needs. It needs the owner's go; no remaining offline check would change this ranking. After it, run the option 2 pair (2 probes, n=2 against the 2 control probes) with the rule written in option 2's test design.

a2.variance_explanation:
Labels: [M] measured from a file stamp or field, [D] derived by arithmetic or regression from measured values, [E] estimated from a stated proxy.

1. The window is output tokens divided by an effective rate, and the rate varies little. [D] Tokens per window-minute (harness-window basis): Grok none 3,945 (86,986 tokens over 22.05 min); Grok 1.21.0 3,787 (274,906 over 72.59); Grok GAS 3,634 (230,327 over 63.38); Luna 3,069 (1,153,899 over 375.9, ledger); Sonnet about 4.9k [E] (about 36k over 7.40). Across a 32-fold range of volume the effective rate moves 1.6-fold (Luna to Sonnet) and 1.2-fold between Luna and Grok. On a log scale, pairwise gaps split like this [D]: Luna vs Grok 1.21.0 (same release, same task, same stage mode; window x5.2): volume x4.20 = 87%, rate x1.23 = 13%. Grok none vs Grok 1.21.0 (x3.3): volume 96.5%, rate 3.5%. Grok GAS vs Grok 1.21.0 (x0.87): volume more than explains it, rate is 4% lower. Luna vs Sonnet (x51): volume about 88%, rate about 12% [E, Sonnet tokens estimated]. Sonnet vs Grok none: volume about 80%, rate about 20% [E]. Volume is the dominant term in every pair I can compute.

2. Host speed (streaming rate). [D] Grok 4.7 medium is the same in all three Grok runs: aggregate 101 to 108 tok/s on responses with under 15% reasoning (n=19, 41, 36), 69.2/69.3/69.6 tok/s on responses over 70% reasoning (n=21, 28, 44), marginal 82 to 90 tok/s on total output tokens (R2 0.88 to 0.92), per-response constant about 0.3 to 1.1 s. Reasoning tokens therefore take about half the generation time (about 48 to 54% [E]) while being 39 to 43% of Grok tokens. Cached context size does not move Grok time: regressing response time on cache_read_input_tokens gives 0.001 to 0.013 s per 1k tokens at contexts of 127k to 205k. Luna: 55.6 tok/s marginal on total tokens plus 2.18 s per response (ledger [M]). Sonnet: about 128 tok/s [D] from 99,115 reported output tokens over 12.93 min of response time; it includes thinking the stream does not expose. Generation throughput therefore ranks Sonnet : Grok : Luna roughly 2.5 : 1.55 : 1. Grok gives part of that back: in the Grok windows 18 to 25% of wall time is not generation (tool and other waits 2.4 / 8.0 / 10.1 min, compactions 1.47 / 5.79 / 5.75 min), against under 1% not in flight on Luna, so the wall-effective gap is 1.2x, not 1.55x. Grok's ShipLoop CLI shell calls took 1.99, 7.45 and 8.81 min in the window (medians 5.5, 1.5, 6.7 s) against about 10 s for all ShipLoop commands on Luna; why the Grok median is 1.5 s in one run and 5.5 to 6.7 s in the other two is unknown (version, machine load and host shell wrapper are confounded; Sonnet's calls were under 1 s on average).

3. What the volume is made of. (a) Improve review. Where the evidence separates it [D]: Grok 1.21.0 45.8 of 71.9 min (63.7%) and 176k of 275k tokens (64.0%); GAS 29.2 of 61.3 min (47.6%) and 103k of 230k tokens (44.9%); Luna 203.4 of 375.0 min (54.1%, tokens not separated); Sonnet 4.05 of 7.32 min (55%, but 2.0 min is a hung command and passes 2 to 3 are stamped); none 0. Time share and token share track each other in Grok. Without Improve the Grok windows would be 26.1 (1.21.0) and 32.1 (GAS) min and none actually took 20.5, so the three Grok authoring-only figures lie within 1.6x of each other while the windows lie within 3.5x. Authoring tokens in the Grok runs are 87.0k (none), 98.9k (1.21.0), 126.9k (GAS); at the measured 3.6 to 3.9k tokens per minute a 30-minute window holds about 109 to 118k [D], so Grok authoring alone sits at the ceiling and Improve is what pushes it over. Pass 1 is 29% of Grok Improve minutes (13.3 of 45.8; 8.4 of 29.2) and the last two confirmation passes per child about 8.0 and 5.7 min; opening and closing are 14% (Grok 1.21.0), 36% (GAS), 14% (Luna). Pass cost differs by host: 1.5 min (Grok 1.21.0) and 1.2 (GAS) against 7.9 on Luna, about 4x more tokens per pass on Luna if the window-average rate holds [E]. (b) Reasoning share: Luna 59.2% vs Grok 38.7 to 43.4%. Luna spent 683k reasoning tokens against 106k (1.21.0), 96k (GAS), 38k (none). (c) Per KB of final planning docs [D]: visible tokens 4.06k (Luna), 2.72k, 2.55k, 1.72k (Grok 1.21.0, GAS, none); reasoning tokens 5.9k, 1.7k, 1.8k, 1.3k. Luna's docs are 116 KB vs 62 / 53 / 29 KB, so about 2x of its volume is document size and the rest is reasoning and visible tokens per byte. (d) Stage hot spots, Luna vs Grok 1.21.0 (authoring before bind unless noted): prepare 14.7 vs 0.65 min, plan 64.1 vs 6.2, test-spec 25.7 vs 1.5, discovery plus research 20.7 vs 4.0, spec 10.4 vs 3.95; Improve plan 56.9 vs 6.0, test-strategy 61.1 vs 14.1. (e) The plan-stage Backchain pass survives planning_review none: 8.38 min and 41% of the none run's tokens, of which about 16% of tokens and 12% of time wrote plan.md and the result.

4. Compaction and context are not what separates the runs. [M] Grok compacts 1, 5, 4 times in its windows (1.2 to 1.5 min each; 6.7%, 8.0%, 9.1% of the window); Luna 10 times (11.55 min, 3.1%). Luna's recovery cost after compaction and kills (17.5 to 20.0 and 10 to 24 min) are ledger upper bounds; I did not measure Grok's re-read cost. Contexts are of the same order (Grok median 127k to 150k, peak about 205k; Luna window 258k, compaction at 240k to 256k).

5. GAS vs Node on Grok 4.7 medium, stage. GAS 61.3 min vs 71.9 (x0.85, n=1 each, within the roughly 2x run-to-run variation the docs report). Tokens 230k vs 275k, 292 vs 323 responses, reasoning 41.5% vs 38.7%, rate 3,634 vs 3,787 per minute. Authoring before binds and other stages is larger on GAS (32.1 vs 26.1 min; 127k vs 99k tokens): the work is a two-hot-seat-player Apps Script app with --delivery-contract (delivery-authority and environment-lifecycle reading, 12 read-only deployment-MCP calls, a spec carrying the deploy guard, 20.6 KB spec and 8.6 KB plan against 19.2 and 4.2), plan-stage Backchain 10.2 vs 6.2 min, spec authoring 7.7 vs 3.95, a pre-engine 1.3 min workspace-start debugging, and a different release (1.22.0/0.54.0 vs 1.21.0/0.53.0), permission mode (default vs auto) and Grok build. Improve is smaller (29.2 vs 45.8 min; 15 vs 26 passes: spec 6 vs 9, test-strategy 4 vs 7, plan 3 vs 4, step-plan 1 vs 3, test-spec 1 vs 3; 7 vs 15 commits). The difference is pass count, which depends on what each review found in that one run; the data cannot say how much is the task and how much is chance.

6. Where the data cannot separate the factors. Model, effort and host are bundled in every run (Luna xhigh, Grok medium, Sonnet unset), so speed is separable but verbosity of the model versus effort level is not. Luna's reasoning is encrypted and Sonnet's thinking is empty, so reasoning content and its necessity are unknown. Sonnet's per-call tokens are unavailable (window tokens are estimated). Improve-specific tokens on Luna were not measured. The cause of Grok's CLI latency spread, of the none run's docs being 41 to 49% of the stage drafts (17 to 20 KB at the first Improve commit), and of the Luna reasoning excess per KB are unknown.
a2.caveats: One run per cell; the committed docs report about 2x run-to-run variation in stage times, so GAS vs Node (15%) and any difference under about 2x between runs is not established. Window definitions: I use engine started to the first W1 test-spec accept (state.md history joined to timeline.json accepted). First-event basis adds 0.1 to 2.1 min (none 22.05, Sonnet 7.40, Node 72.59, GAS 63.38, Luna 375.9); LEARNINGS gives 63.8 for GAS from harness launch. Method checks: my bind-mtime Improve split reproduces the ledger exactly on Luna (44.5/61.1/56.9/26.7/14.2 = 203.4, opening 26.3, 84,886 B of review notes over 22 passes), and the Grok 1.21.0 split reproduces run-doc-grok-medium-v1210.json; Grok response time was derived from stamped tool_call_update to usage events, and generation plus waits plus compaction sums to the last response end within 0.01 min. Reasoning tokens are treated as a subset of output tokens: reasoning never exceeds output in 1,378 Grok responses (max ratio 0.985), but the stream does not say so. Luna figures (tokens, decode rate, compaction, kills) are from ledger-account-final.json and stage-clock.md, not re-derived from the rollouts. Sonnet window tokens are an estimate (about 36k) and its decode rate (about 128 tok/s) includes unmeasured thinking; compactions are unmeasured on that host. The commit-per-pass mapping is ambiguous by one pass per child, so I only claim 'at least N passes changed no file' from commit counts. The GAS run is a different release, permission mode and harness from the Node runs; the none run read at analysis time shows status done, which I did not grade. What these data say about one-shot-and-fix-later is observational only: the one none run finished 52 of 52 actions with no revise, but with planning docs under half the stage-mode size and no matched stage-mode run on the same release; the Luna replan (165.9 min) escaped review, so review is not shown to catch it; no run varies Improve alone. No process was touched and no model-backed run was started. Scratch scripts: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-dadleet-src-skill-craft/f7d9360d-b88d-417b-8773-fc5b3eee6419/scratchpad/planning-waste/ (stages.py, improve_split.py, grok_events.py, analyze_grok.py, split_tokens.py, passes2.py, sonnet.py, tools.py).

a3.what_later_stages_relied_on:
What later stages relied on. Mostly not the prose of the planning documents. In noneLive, delivery-phase tool calls (562) named one of the five planning documents or the step-plan result file in 28 reads and 9 searches (6.6%), against 91 writes or edits that are carry-forward, document and result submissions (measured: path match on tool_call rawInput in events.jsonl). The reliance runs through machine-read fields: the step plan's test_commands (command, suite, ids, min_tests, criteria, paths) become the exit conditions of test-author, test-green, regression, verify and system-test, and the ids originate in the test strategy and test spec; 50 script verification receipts exist across noneLive, sonnetStage and GAS and 48 passed, the two failures being engine-versus-document interactions (node:test uncounted, the word 'pending'). Spec R-ids all appear in the test strategy in every run (presence only) and product-acceptance cites TC ids per request sentence. Review-added content was consumed in three observed places (Sonnet listen guard and createServer seam, GAS fence exit codes quoted by both baselines, Luna F-TEST and D-9 vectors in the W1 tests). Backchain records had 0 delivery reads in noneLive.

What the evidence supports. (1) The script-checkable planning products (ids, commands, paths, probes) are load-bearing: later gates can only check what planning named. (2) The model review of planning documents bought real fixes, concentrated in pass 1 (first pass changed files in 4 of 5 Luna children, about 4 of 5 Grok, 5 of 5 Sonnet), at about 1 min per fix on Sonnet, about 4 on GAS, about 10 on Grok and about 20 to 45 on Luna (derived: minutes over the ledger's and the investigation's counts); later passes were mostly confirmations or churn (Luna 10 of 22 no change, Grok's four-commit allow-list chain, Sonnet 10 of 15 trivial). (3) On fast hosts every defect found after planning was repaired inside the stage that produced it in about 1 to 3 minutes (noneLive, Sonnet, GAS), with no revise on noneLive or GAS and one 1.9-minute revise on Sonnet. (4) The costly escapes were on Luna, 165.9 and 123.5 min, and both were contradictions between planning text and test code about a loadable module or helper contract, reported by the model at test-red or implement, not by a script. Their cost is the redo path: the replan step-plan was 120.1 min, of which Backchain 41.2 and Improve 69.5, so a later fix is expensive largely because it re-runs planning stages with their loops; derived under none the Improve part would not run. (5) The 0.54.0 engine moved that class earlier and cheaper: a step-plan packet sentence and the test-author probe (PROBE_RULE), added after the Luna runs. (6) A planning review plausibly catches, with analogues in other runs: contradictions between spec lines (Grok R-1 vs R-6), under-specified oracles (Grok follow-up cell vs noneLive TC-12), platform claims (GAS 41233ce, E6b 10 of 15, vs noneLive 'ESM'), fail-open checks (GAS a38e7e7). It cannot catch engine-internal behaviour (the node:test reader gap that Sonnet's own step-plan review looked at and approved; the skip-word list) nor defects in code written after planning (TC-8 draft, TC-15 hole, malformed-target crash, oversized body). (7) Net for 'one-shot and fix later': on these hosts the later gates repaired the leftover defects in minutes, and the none window was 22.0 min against 72.7 min for Grok in stage mode (one run each, confounded). The break-even in docs/shiploop-planning-review-plan-2026-10-05.md, 1.2 to 3.0 extra escapes per Luna run, is an arithmetic bound, not a measurement.

What the evidence cannot support. It cannot support a claim that planning review is worthless or worthwhile in general: there is no paired, same-model, same-version comparison of stage against none; no blind quality comparison; no run of none on Luna; no run that reached the late stages after a reviewed plan on Grok (grokStageNode stopped at baseline; GAS stopped before system-test); and the escape rate without review is unmeasured, not zero. It also cannot attribute the none window's speed to removing review alone, and it cannot say whether Backchain's one pass earned its 8.4 minutes in noneLive.
